Software Engineering Lab 2: Agile Backlog Creation & Sprint Simulation in Jira

Personalized Meal & Diet Subscription Manager (Problem Statement #19, Healthcare & Telemedicine) Jira project: Diet Subscription Manager (DSM), a company-managed Scrum project.

1. Scope and Source Requirements

This lab converts the Lab 1 requirements for the Personalized Meal & Diet Subscription Manager into an Agile backlog and runs it through two sprints in Jira.

Lab 1 Req Description Priority Backlog item
FR-001 Generate weekly plans within macro constraints and allergen exclusions High DSM-6, DSM-7
FR-002 Create and update a health profile (allergens, calorie goal, carb limit) High DSM-4, DSM-5
FR-003 Dietitian approves/rejects each plan, reason required on rejection High DSM-8, DSM-9
FR-004 Pause/skip/reschedule a delivery; reject inside the 12-hour cut-off High DSM-10, DSM-11
FR-005 Record delivery outcome with timestamp, visible to subscriber and dietitian Medium DSM-12
NFR-001 Schedule modifications performant and authenticated up to the cut-off High DSM-11
NFR-002 Health data encrypted at rest, access-controlled, audited High Constraint on DSM-4/5

2. Epics

Key Epic Covers Requirements
DSM-1 Health Profile & Meal Plan Generation A subscriber records their dietary constraints and the system builds a compliant weekly menu from them. FR-001, FR-002, NFR-002
DSM-2 Dietitian Plan Review & Approval No meal plan reaches a subscriber until a dietitian has signed it off. FR-003
DSM-3 Delivery Scheduling & Fulfilment Tracking Subscribers change upcoming deliveries within the kitchen's cut-off; the system records what was delivered. FR-004, FR-005, NFR-001

3. User Stories, Story Points and Priority

Key Epic User Story Priority Points Traces to
DSM-4 DSM-1 Create health profile — As a subscriber, I want to enter my allergen exclusions, daily calorie goal and carbohydrate limit, so that my meal plans are built around my medical constraints. High 5 FR-002
DSM-6 DSM-1 Generate weekly meal plan — As a subscriber, I want the system to generate a 7-day menu from my saved profile, so that I do not have to plan meals for the week myself. High 8 FR-001
DSM-7 DSM-1 Block excluded allergens from a plan — As a subscriber with a food allergy, I want the system to reject any recipe containing an allergen on my exclusion list, so that I am never served something unsafe. High 5 FR-001
DSM-8 DSM-2 View plans awaiting review — As a dietitian, I want to see a queue of draft plans waiting on me, so that I can work through them before subscribers are left waiting. High 3 FR-003
DSM-9 DSM-2 Approve or reject a plan with a reason — As a dietitian, I want to approve a draft plan, or reject it with a written reason, so that an unsafe plan is never released to the subscriber. High 5 FR-003
DSM-10 DSM-3 Skip or pause an upcoming delivery — As a subscriber, I want to skip or pause a delivery that is already scheduled, so that I am not sent food I will not be there to eat. High 5 FR-004
DSM-5 DSM-1 Update health profile — As a subscriber, I want to edit my allergens and calorie goal at any time, so that my plans stay correct when my diet changes. Medium 3 FR-002
DSM-11 DSM-3 Enforce the 12-hour change cut-off — As a kitchen manager, I want schedule changes made less than 12 hours before dispatch to be refused, so that we do not waste food already procured. Medium 3 FR-004, NFR-001
DSM-12 DSM-3 Record delivery outcome — As a delivery agent, I want to mark each delivery as Delivered, Failed or Not Attempted with a timestamp, so that the subscriber and dietitian can see what arrived. Medium 3 FR-005

Total: 40 story points across 9 stories.

Estimating with planning poker

Story points measure relative effort, not hours. The Fibonacci scale is used because the gaps widen as the numbers grow, which forces a decision instead of an argument between a 6 and a 7. In a team setting each member reveals a card at the same time so nobody anchors on the loudest voice; where the cards diverge, the two extremes explain their reasoning and the round is re-run.

DSM-6 is the only 8. Generating a weekly menu is not one operation: it is constraint solving over a recipe set, seven days of totals to balance, and a fallback when no compliant menu exists.

Prioritising and ranking the backlog

Priority follows user impact, not convenience. A requirement whose failure is a clinical safety incident outranks one whose failure is an inconvenience, which puts allergen exclusion (DSM-7) and dietitian approval (DSM-9) at High.

The backlog was then reordered so that rank matches priority: all six High stories above the three Medium ones, dependency order preserved inside each band. Both sprints pull from the top of that list. One consequence is that DSM-5 is Medium, so it ranks below all six High stories and lands in Sprint 2 despite sharing an epic with DSM-4.

4. Sprint Execution

Two sprints, one week each. Both were simulated: stories were moved To Do → In Progress → Done within a single session, so the sprint duration is one week while the recorded activity is compressed into minutes. This shows up in the shape of the burndown chart.

Sprint 1

Goal: A subscriber can set up a dietary profile and get a compliant weekly plan that a dietitian can approve or reject.

Key Story Points Outcome
DSM-4 Create health profile 5 Done
DSM-6 Generate weekly meal plan 8 Not completed — carried over
DSM-7 Block excluded allergens from a plan 5 Done
DSM-8 View plans awaiting review 3 Done
DSM-9 Approve or reject a plan with a reason 5 Done

Committed 26. Delivered 18. Carried over 8.

The goal was only partly met. Profile setup, allergen validation and the dietitian review path shipped, but the plan generation they exist to serve did not, so Sprint 1 ended with an empty review queue and nothing to approve.

Sprint 2

Goal: Finish weekly plan generation, let subscribers change an upcoming delivery, and allow profile edits to flow into the next plan.

Key Story Points Outcome
DSM-6 Generate weekly meal plan (carried over) 8 Done
DSM-10 Skip or pause an upcoming delivery 5 Done
DSM-5 Update health profile 3 Done

Committed 16. Delivered 16. Sprint 2 was planned smaller, taking the carry-over first. The goal was met in full.

Progress comments

Progress went into comments on the issues, not only into status changes, so the board carries the reasoning as well as the outcome. The comment that matters is on DSM-6, written once it was clear it would not finish:

"Not finishing this sprint. The generator builds a compliant single day, but balancing a full week inside the calorie tolerance still fails on roughly one profile in four, and there is no fallback yet for when no compliant menu exists. Carrying over to Sprint 2. In hindsight this should have been split into three stories at planning rather than estimated as one 8."

Position after two sprints

Points Stories
Delivered 34 7
Remaining in backlog 6 2 (DSM-11, DSM-12)
Total 40 9

Velocity: 18, then 16.

5. Reflection

Did the estimations reflect the actual effort?

Mostly, with one miss. The 3s and 5s behaved as estimated. DSM-6 at 8 was under-estimated rather than mis-sized: the 8 signalled uncertainty, but the estimate still assumed plan generation was a single story. It was not, and it should have been split. Once it was split in Sprint 2 it finished without difficulty.

A large Fibonacci number is a signal to split a story, not a label for a big one.

Was the backlog well-prioritised?

Yes. Priority followed user impact, the backlog was ranked to match, and both sprints pulled from the top. The two safety-critical stories, DSM-7 and DSM-9, shipped inside the first two sprints; the two still outstanding are both Medium. Nothing High is left undone.

One ordering choice is arguable. DSM-8 was pulled into Sprint 1 alongside the plan generation it depends on, so when DSM-6 slipped it shipped into a system with no plans to review. Ranking by impact is right; sequencing a dependent story into the same sprint as its dependency is a risk that should have been visible at planning time.

How did the simulated sprint align with the plan?

Sprint 1 did not: 26 committed, 18 delivered, with the largest story missing. Sprint 2 aligned exactly at 16 and 16, partly because it was planned after watching Sprint 1 miss.

Two sprints is too small a sample for a stable velocity, but 18 and 16 suggest a real capacity near 17 points, against the 26 initially committed.

What did the burndown chart show about capacity?

The event log is where the burndown is legible:

Event Burned Remaining
Sprint start, 5 stories added — 26
DSM-4 completed 5 21
DSM-7 completed 5 16
DSM-8 completed 3 13
DSM-9 completed 5 8
Sprint ended — 8 (DSM-6 unfinished)

The line stops at 8 and never reaches the axis. That gap is the capacity finding: a commitment roughly 44% above what was delivered.

The plotted curve is less informative, and the reason matters. The To Do → In Progress → Done moves were all made inside one session, so every event lands in the first few minutes of a seven-day axis and the line renders as a near-vertical drop rather than a staircase beside the guideline. That is an artifact of the simulation, not a property of the plan.

In a real sprint that shape would be a warning sign, and for one story it was: DSM-6 was too large to close incrementally.

What the team would take into the next sprint

  1. Split anything estimated at 8 or above before committing to it. DSM-6 is the whole argument.
  2. Do not put a story in the same sprint as the work it depends on unless that dependency finishes early. DSM-8 delivered nothing usable for a week.
  3. Commit to about 17 points, not 26, until there is velocity history to justify more.
